# Learning to sail at thirty-four

The first thing my instructor told me was that the boat wants to go. This
struck me as mystical nonsense at the time. I had spent the morning being
shouted at about a rope, and nothing about the arrangement suggested that
anything wanted anything.

She was right, though, in a narrow and mechanical way. A sail is a wing turned
on its side. Air moving across it produces lift, the keel converts most of that
sideways push into forward motion, and the boat goes. You do not make it go.
You stop preventing it.

What took me a whole summer to learn was how much of sailing is subtraction.
The novice instinct is to pull things tighter. Tight sail, tight grip, tight
jaw. Everything I did with force made the boat slower and me more tired. The
people who were quick were doing almost nothing, and doing it slightly earlier
than I did.

There is a moment, usually about forty minutes into a good afternoon, when the
heel settles and the noise drops and the wake goes quiet behind you. Sailors
call it being in the groove. It is not a spiritual state. It is what happens
when the sail shape, the rudder angle, and your weight all stop arguing with
each other. It lasts until the wind shifts, which is usually about ninety
seconds.

I still cannot dock. Docking is a separate discipline, apparently, involving
judgement about momentum that I have not acquired and possibly cannot. My
instructor has stopped shouting about it, which I choose to read as progress
rather than resignation.
